options.text: 'Rents rose 40%, which is significant.'
'Rents rose 40% last year.'
'Rents rose 40%, from £500 to £700.'
'Rents rose by 40 percent.'

questions.explanation: Stating the base and new value makes the percentage meaningful. Time, judgement, or repetition do not help.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A trend line drawn through three points
questions.learningObjective: Explain why three points are unreliable
questions.stem: Why is a trend line through three points unreliable?

answer.exemplar: Three points cannot separate a genuine trend from random variation, so the line may reflect noise rather than a lasting pattern.

questions.explanation: Three points cannot separate trend from noise. The line may reflect chance rather than a pattern.
questions.hint: Noise can look like a trend.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A headline wider than the story
questions.learningObjective: Revise an overbroad headline

stimulus.body: Headline: 'City in Crisis.' Story: one delayed bridge repair, two weeks behind schedule. No other projects affected. The repair will finish next month.

questions.stem: Which headline better matches the story?

options.text: 'City in Crisis.'
'Bridge Repair Two Weeks Behind Schedule.'
'City Faces Widespread Delays.'
'Bridge Repair Delayed.'

questions.explanation: The precise headline matches the story's scope. Keeping or inflating the overbroad headline misleads; vagueness is weaker.
questions.hint: Match headline to the actual event.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A superlative with nothing to compare
questions.learningObjective: Detect an unsupported superlative

stimulus.body: The memo calls the proposal 'the best' for the city. No alternatives are listed. Costs are not compared. The memo recommends approval.

questions.stem: What is the superlative's problem?

options.text: The proposal may cost too much.
The word 'best' is too informal.
It lacks a stated comparison set.
Superlatives are never allowed.

questions.explanation: The superlative lacks a comparison set. Register, cost, or blanket bans miss the missing basis.
questions.hint: Name what it is best among.

questions.explanation: Showing the absolute base and new count removes the deception. Repeating or inflating keeps it hidden.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A contested allegation with no reply
questions.learningObjective: Identify an allegation without a reply
questions.stem: Which memo contains an uncontested allegation?

options.text: A memo quoting both sides of a dispute.
A memo with cost estimates and no allegations.
A memo alleging fraud with no response included.
A memo with no quotations at all.
options.misconception: confuses absence of quotes with allegation

questions.explanation: An allegation with no response is uncontested in the memo. Data-only, balanced, or quote-free memos are not allegations.
questions.hint: Look for an allegation lacking a reply.

questions.explanation: Limiting the claim to the month and noting the need for more data fixes the overgeneralisation. The other options keep or extend the overclaim.

questions.learningObjective: Detect a missing denominator

stimulus.body: The memo says '40% of respondents support the plan.' It does not state how many were surveyed. The plan affects 50,000 residents. The survey was online.

options.text: The residents' names.
The number of respondents surveyed.
The survey's website address.
The plan's cost.

questions.explanation: The denominator (respondents surveyed) is missing. Names, URLs, or cost do not make the percentage meaningful.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A trend line drawn through three points
questions.learningObjective: Place a trend claim in context

stimulus.body: Accidents were 12, 15, and 18 over three years. A planner predicted 21 for next year. The data cover one junction. Weather varied.

questions.stem: What caveat should accompany the prediction?

options.text: The data are useless.
The prediction is certainly accurate.
The prediction rests on three points from one junction and may not hold.
Weather is irrelevant.

questions.explanation: The prediction rests on three points from one junction and may not hold. Certainty, dismissal, or ignoring confounders misjudge the evidence.
questions.hint: State the limits of the data.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a small base misleads
questions.stem: Why does a relative figure hide a small base?

answer.exemplar: A relative figure hides a small base because 'doubled' sounds large even when the absolute rise is tiny, so readers overestimate the change.

questions.explanation: Relative language sounds large even for tiny absolute changes, misleading readers about scale.
